candidates.speaker: Trent Horn
candidates.proposition: Contingent reality requires an explanation beyond the entire collection of contingent things.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Trent the opening statement, and Trent presents this numbered argument continuously in the first person.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This establishes the explanatory principle and necessary external terminus on which the subsequent identification of a divine cause depends.
candidates.contextSummary: After announcing a nine-question positive case, Trent distinguishes contingent things from their explanations, defends sufficient reason, rejects an infinite contingent regress, and infers an explanation beyond the contingent universe.

candidates.speaker: Trent Horn
candidates.proposition: The universe does not explain itself because existence is not a necessary property of universes.
candidates.attributionBasis: Trent identifies this as his second numbered question and supplies the triangle comparison as his own supporting argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Rejecting the universe as a necessary self-explanatory entity is essential to locating the required explanation outside the universe itself.
candidates.contextSummary: Trent contrasts a triangle's essential three-sidedness with its contingent color and argues that asking why the universe exists remains intelligible, indicating that universes do not exist by necessity.

candidates.speaker: Trent Horn
candidates.proposition: Change requires a purely actual first actualizer rather than an infinite series of derivative actualizers.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening statement and explicit transition to the property of change firmly identify Trent as the source.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The act-and-potency argument supplies a first cause characterized as pure actuality and excludes the changing universe from being that cause.
candidates.contextSummary: Trent analyzes change as potential becoming actual, argues that derivative actualizers cannot constitute a sufficient infinite series, and concludes that a purely actual cause must ground change.

candidates.speaker: Trent Horn
candidates.proposition: An infinite past causal history is contradictory, so the universe began and requires an uncaused cause.
candidates.attributionBasis: Trent introduces the universe's finite past and develops the paper-passer argument without any intervening speaker change.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies an independent route from the alleged impossibility of infinite causal histories to a finite past and uncaused necessary source.
candidates.contextSummary: Using the paper-passer scenario and related paradoxes, Trent argues that causal histories cannot be infinite, infers a finite past, and consolidates the resulting cause as necessary, uncaused, and purely actual.

candidates.speaker: Trent Horn
candidates.proposition: The first cause must be changeless, timeless, immaterial, unlimited in power, and necessarily existent.
candidates.attributionBasis: Trent proceeds through numbered questions three through seven, explicitly deriving each attribute of the previously inferred cause.
candidates.loadBearingReason: These deductions connect the generic first cause to several traditional divine attributes central to the affirmative case that the cause is God.
candidates.contextSummary: Trent derives changelessness from pure actuality, timelessness from changelessness, immateriality from transcendence of space and time, unlimited power from unrestricted actuality, and necessity from independence and incapacity for nonexistence.

candidates.speaker: Trent Horn
candidates.proposition: The universe's cause is personal and all-knowing rather than an abstract or impersonal explanatory entity.
candidates.attributionBasis: Trent labels this his eighth question and enumerates five considerations for a personal cause in one continuous presentation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Personality and knowledge are indispensable to the transition from a metaphysical first cause to the traditional conception of God defended by the pro side.
candidates.contextSummary: Trent argues that causal efficacy excludes abstract objects, that creation from nothing calls for an agent explanation, that necessary abstract truths require a necessary mind, and that divine explanation is preferable to brute origination.

candidates.speaker: Trent Horn
candidates.proposition: Objective moral facts support a supremely good divine source and therefore support God's existence.
candidates.attributionBasis: Trent introduces the moral dimension as his final numbered question and explicitly states and defends a moral-realism syllogism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The moral argument directly concludes that God exists and supplies the goodness attribute required by Trent's cumulative identification of the first cause.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Alex's previously stated account of moral truths as consequences of subjective well-being assumptions.

candidates.contextSummary: Trent argues that pure actuality lacks defect, presents moral realism as evidence for God, appeals to apparently objective moral truths, and challenges Alex's well-being account with a hypothetical involving engineered willing slaves.

candidates.speaker: Trent Horn
candidates.proposition: Moral responsibility and the wrongness of punishing innocents require free will and a divine moral foundation.
candidates.attributionBasis: Trent explicitly attributes determinism to Alex and then advances a sustained objection concerning blame and punishment.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument challenges the con speaker's determinism while reinforcing the affirmative claim that objective moral responsibility requires divine grounding.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Alex's position that physical events, including human actions, are determined by prior physical causes.

candidates.contextSummary: Trent contends that determinism would make blaming offenders analogous to blaming natural forces and could permit instrumental punishment of innocents, contrary to objective facts about responsibility and justice.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: Apparently gratuitous animal suffering is more expected under naturalism and seriously undermines belief in a loving, just God.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the opening statement to Alex, who expressly identifies animal suffering as his affirmative case and develops it continuously.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Alex presents animal suffering as his principal positive reason against Christian theism and contrasts its evidential fit under theism and naturalism.
candidates.contextSummary: Alex argues that a loving God could permit no more suffering than necessary, uses an unseen deer's prolonged agony to press the possibility of gratuitous suffering, notes the absence of clear animal compensation, and says such suffering fits naturalism better.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: Heaven would show that free will can exist without suffering, defeating the claim that freedom requires permission for grave evil.
candidates.attributionBasis: Alex explicitly turns to the standard free-will defense, poses his heaven objection to Trent, and completes it in the delivered lookahead.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This counterexample directly attacks a major theistic explanation of moral evil by alleging a possible realm containing freedom without corresponding suffering.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The theistic free-will defense that preventing severe moral evil would be incompatible with genuine human freedom.

candidates.contextSummary: Alex grants for argument that love requires freedom, then asks whether heaven contains both free will and unrestricted wrongdoing; if it contains freedom without suffering, he argues the same combination is possible on earth.
